punctuated: 如手就樹，堅而不敧也；四矢既均，而皆貫乎革，如手就樹，正而不偏也。省括于度，藝固精矣，猶必無憮無傲，不以己之中而驕者為可尚焉；發彼有的，射固善矣，猶必無偕立、無踰言，不以人之不中而傲者為可貴焉。非射於終而尚德乎？夫既射以為樂矣，而燕猶未終也，曾孫為主，復登筵焉，可不酌酒以為頌乎？斯時也，獻爵尚多，則旨酒思柔，而汁滓維厚也；舉觶無筭，則大斗是酌，而器用如式也。然飲此旨酒，豈為口腹之飲而已乎？以頤養天和，頭髪白復黄，面如凍梨，而獲壽之徵焉；酌此大斗，豈為飲食之具而已乎？以保養天倪，願黄耇既介，背有台文，而得壽之兆焉。又非飲於終而祝壽乎？吁！射雖終而禮猶飭，飲將終而祝益隆，王者之於父兄耆老，何其情有加而意無窮也歟！抑王者之燕親親，既曰「以祈黄耇」、「黄耇台背」，又曰「以引以翼，以介景福」，是不徒有福，而有德以享其壽也；及《既醉》之答君，既曰「君子萬年，介爾景福」，又曰「高朗令終，令終有俶」，是不徒有其始，而又有以善其終也。上以是施之，下以是報之，忠厚之意溢於言表，
translation_en:
…as if planted by hand, firm and unleaning; the four arrows are evenly placed and all pierce the leather target, as if planted by hand, straight and unskewed. Examining the nock according to the rule, their skill is certainly refined; yet what is to be esteemed is that they must show neither insolence nor arrogance, not growing proud because they hit the mark. Shooting at that target, their archery is certainly good; yet what is to be valued is that they must neither stand out of turn nor speak out of bounds, not growing haughty because others missed the mark. Is this not conducting archery at the close of the feast while exalting virtue?

Now, having conducted the archery for pleasure, the feast is still not yet over. The distant descendant acts as host and once more ascends the mat; how could he not pour wine to offer a toast of praise? At this moment, the goblets presented are still many, so the fine wine is mild and rich in its brew; the cups raised are beyond count, so it is ladled with the great dipper, and the vessels used conform to the proper standard. Yet in drinking this fine wine, how could it be merely drink for the mouth and belly? It is to nourish natural harmony, so that white hair turns yellow again and the face becomes like a frosted pear, thereby obtaining the signs of longevity. And in ladling with this great dipper, how could it be merely an implement for food and drink? It is to preserve natural vitality, wishing that hoary old age be granted and the back bear the markings of the globe-fish, thereby gaining the omens of longevity. Is this not, moreover, drinking at the close of the feast while praying for long life?

Ah! Though the archery has ended, ritual propriety is still strictly maintained; as the drinking draws to a close, the prayers for blessing grow ever more abundant. In the true king's treatment of his paternal uncles, elder brothers, and aged elders, how deepening is his affection and how boundless his regard! Moreover, when the true king feasts his kin, the ode not only says, "to pray for hoary old age" and "hoary old age with a mottled back," but also says, "leading them on and supporting them, so as to increase their great blessings"—meaning that they do not merely possess good fortune, but possess the virtue whereby to enjoy their longevity. And when the ode "Already Drunk" (Jizui) replies to the ruler, it not only says, "May the lord live for ten thousand years, and may your great blessings be increased," but also says, "Lofty and brilliant, leading to a good end; and a good end has its beginning"—meaning that he not only has a good beginning, but also has the means to perfect his end. The superior bestows this upon those below, and those below repay the superior with this; a spirit of loyal generosity overflows beyond the words, …

text:

成湯自彼氐羌莫敢不來享莫敢不來王曰
商是常天命多辟設都于禹之績歲事來辟
勿予禍適稼穡匪懈天命降監下民有嚴不
僭不濫不敢怠遑

「有截其所，湯孫之緒。維女荆楚，居國南鄉。昔有成湯，自彼氐羌，莫敢不來享，莫敢不來王，曰商是常。天命多辟，設都于禹之績。歲事來辟，勿予禍適，稼穡匪懈。天命降監，下民有嚴，不僭不濫，不敢怠遑。」

王鏊

同考試官教諭原批：此題頗長，本難包括，作者多失旨。是篇辭語圓活，理脉亦貫，說出高宗所以中興之義，詳悉無遺，必老學之士也，宜冠本房。

同考試官學正胡批：此題前三章言高宗中興之業，後一章所以致中興之道，作者往往分截無定見。是篇深合題意，而詞足以發之，《葩經》之翹楚也。

考試官修撰鄭批：發越詳盡。

考試官左諭德謝批：長題貴該括，是作得之。

商人頌先王能振中興之業，必推其所以致中興之道。盖伐遠而諸侯服，此高宗中興之業也；自非畏天人而公刑賞，奚能然哉？詩人頌高宗中興之盛如此。
translation_en:
… Is this not why the house of Zhou flourished so!

"Brought cleanly into order was their place—the continuing achievement of Tang's descendant. 'You people of Jing-Chu, dwelling in the southern region of the state: in the days of Cheng Tang of old, even from the distant Di and Qiang, none dared not come to present offerings, none dared not come to pay homage to the king, saying: "This is the constant rule of Shang."' Heaven commanded the many rulers, establishing their capitals within the bounds of Yu's labors. For the annual affairs they come before the sovereign: 'Do not visit us with calamity or reproof; we have not been remiss in our husbandry.' Heaven's mandate looks down in inspection; the people below are to be held in awe—neither erring in rewards nor excessive in punishments, not daring to be indolent or at ease." [Book of Odes, "Yin Wu"]

Wang Ao 王鏊

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Yuan: This topic passage is quite long and inherently difficult to encompass as a whole, so most candidates missed its main purport. In this essay the phrasing is supple and lively, and the thread of reasoning is coherent throughout. It brings out the significance of how Gaozong achieved his dynastic restoration in full detail, leaving nothing out. He must be a scholar of mature learning, and deserves to be placed first in my examination ward.

Comment by Associate Examiner Director of Studies Hu: The first three stanzas of this topic speak of the enterprise of Gaozong's restoration, while the final stanza speaks of the way by which that restoration was brought about; candidates often divide the passage arbitrarily without a settled view. This essay deeply accords with the meaning of the topic, and its diction suffices to bring it forth—an outstanding specimen among the candidates in the Classic of Poetry.

Comment by Examiner Senior Compiler Zheng: Expressive, spirited, and thoroughly detailed.

Comment by Examiner Left Admonisher Xie: In a long topic, what is prized is comprehensive grasp; this composition has achieved it.

When the people of Shang praised their former king for being able to rouse the enterprise of dynastic restoration, they necessarily traced the way by which he brought that restoration about. For to chastise the distant and make the feudal lords submit—this was the enterprise of Gaozong's restoration; yet had he not stood in awe of Heaven and man and been impartial in punishments and rewards, how could it have been so? Such was the way the poet praised the flourishing of Gaozong's restoration. …

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
是詩以為祀高宗之樂歌蓋謂高宗憤荆楚之叛奮
神武之威盡平其地截然齊一而不得以紊我疆土
者果誰之功歟皆我湯孫神武之功也盡平其民斬
然整齊而不得毒我人民者伊誰之力歟皆我湯孫
深入之力也既伐之以威必責之以義意謂維汝荆
楚之遠亦居吾國之南昔我成湯之世遠如氐羌之
夷亦莫敢不獻琛而來享莫敢不稽首而來王曰此
有商之常禮也况汝荆楚曷敢不至哉荆楚既平諸
侯自服由是天命諸侯各建都於禹所治之地莫不
===
三年一聘以祈王之不譴五年一朝以祈王之不謫
曰我之稼穡不敢解也庶可以免咎矣夫以夷夏同
心歸服如此果何自而然耶蓋以天聰明自我民聰
明是天命降監在民則下民亦有嚴矣天明畏自我
民明畏是天命下視在民則下民亦可畏矣高宗知
其然故於賞也則奉天命而不僭於刑也則奉天討
而不濫既不僭矣而兢惕之心不敢怠不以私喜而
移也既不濫矣而恭嚴之心不敢遑不以私怒而渝
也高宗畏天人而公刑賞如此則其所以平遠人服

translation_en:
…this ode as a liturgical song for sacrificing to Gaozong. It means to say: Gaozong, indignant at the rebellion of Jing-Chu, roused the might of his divine martial valor and completely pacified their territory, bringing it into crisp, uniform order so that they could no longer throw our borders into confusion—whose achievement was this, indeed? It was entirely the achievement of the divine martial valor of our Tang's descendant! He completely pacified their people, bringing them into strict, orderly alignment so that they could no longer harm our populace—whose strength was this, indeed? It was entirely the strength of the deep campaign of our Tang's descendant!

Having struck them with awe, he necessarily rebuked them with righteousness, meaning to say: "Though you of Jing-Chu are distant, you still dwell in the south of our realm. Formerly, in the age of our Cheng Tang, even barbarians as distant as the Di and Qiang none of them dared not present treasures and come to offer tribute, and none dared not bow their heads to the ground and come to acknowledge the king's suzerainty, saying: 'This is the constant ritual of the house of Shang.' How much less should you of Jing-Chu dare not come?"

Once Jing-Chu was pacified, the feudal lords naturally submitted. Thereupon the feudal lords, bearing the Mandate of Heaven, each established their capitals in the lands regulated by Yu. None failed to send a mission of inquiry every three years to pray that the king would not reprimand them, or to come to court every five years to pray that the king would not censure them, saying: "We dare not be remiss in our husbandry; perhaps by this we may escape blame."

Now, that barbarian and Chinese alike submitted with one heart in this manner—from what, indeed, did this arise? It was because Heaven's hearing and seeing proceed from our people's hearing and seeing; since Heaven's Mandate looks down and inspects through the people, the common people below also possess majesty. Heaven's discernment of the virtuous and punishment of the wicked proceed from our people's discernment and punishment; since Heaven's Mandate looks down through the people, the common people below are also to be held in awe. Knowing this to be so, in his rewards Gaozong upheld Heaven's Mandate and did not overstep; in his punishments he upheld Heaven's chastisement and was not excessive. Already free from overstepping, his cautious and fearful heart still dared not grow lax, nor was it swayed by private joy; already free from excess, his reverent and stern heart still dared not take ease, nor was it altered by private anger. Because Gaozong stood in awe of Heaven and man and was impartial in punishments and rewards like this, that by which he pacified distant peoples and brought into submission…

… the feudal lords! Alas, the rise of kingly enterprise is no accident. Founding a dynasty is certainly difficult, and preserving what has been achieved is not easy; how much more so for a monarch of dynastic revival who inherits the aftermath of decline and weakness—there has never been one who did not prevail through martial virtue! Thus Gaozong, majestic and resplendent, remade the state of Yin. Truly, he was worthy of being the grandson of Tang, and worthy of being a lord of dynastic revival! Rightly did later generations establish for him a temple never to be removed for a hundred generations, thereby praising his flourishing virtue, announcing his accomplished merit, and offering sacrifice to him. Oh, how glorious!

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
"The Earl of Zheng fled home without joining the covenant." [Fifth year of Duke Xi.] "The Duke met the Grand宰 Duke of Zhou, the Marquis of Qi, the Viscount of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao at Kuiqiu." [Ninth year of Duke Xi.]

Comment by Examiner, Left Admonisher Xie: The writing has decisive judgment.

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
義耶盖惠王有易子之心桓公有首止之歃君子於
此必曰子鄭吾君之子也且為世子吾君之命也諸
侯盟首止以定其位實所以尊王命而定王儲也奚
可昧厥義耶夫何鄭伯徇撫汝之私命棄儀衛而逃
歸彼徒知王命之當從而義之可否不能審也春秋
得不深貶之哉故曰從私命而不制以義者為可譏
以此至若周公承命以賜級齊桓違命而下拜春秋
善何而美其能制以義耶盖襄王有惠養老臣之恩
周公將加勞賜級之命常人於此必曰下拜禮也無
===
下拜命也從寵命而不下拜未為泰也孰克制以義
耶幸而齊桓則凜然天威咫尺之敬慓然下拜登受
之恭彼惟知臣節之不可虧而王命之違否不暇顧
也春秋得不深美之哉故曰違寵命而能制以義者
為可美以此吁命從楚而從楚者君驕而臣諂也命
無拜而下拜者君仁而臣敬也春秋君臣之賢否得
失不亦於此可見乎雖然鄭伯逃歸未幾而有乞盟
之舉則其悔悟深切可知矣桓公葵丘無何而有緣
陵之專封則其不能終守臣節可見噫鄭文之庸陋

punctuated: 義耶？盖惠王有易子之心，桓公有首止之歃，君子於此，必曰：「子鄭，吾君之子也；且為世子，吾君之命也。諸侯盟首止以定其位，實所以尊王命而定王儲也，奚可昧厥義耶？」夫何鄭伯徇「撫汝」之私命，棄儀衛而逃歸？彼徒知王命之當從，而義之可否不能審也，春秋得不深貶之哉？故曰：從私命而不制以義者為可譏，以此。至若周公承命以賜級，齊桓違命而下拜，春秋善何而美其能制以義耶？盖襄王有惠養老臣之恩，周公將加勞賜級之命，常人於此，必曰：「下拜，禮也；無下拜，命也。從寵命而不下拜，未為泰也。」孰克制以義耶？幸而齊桓則凜然天威咫尺之敬，慓然下拜登受之恭。彼惟知臣節之不可虧，而王命之違否不暇顧也，春秋得不深美之哉？故曰：違寵命而能制以義者為可美，以此。吁！命從楚而從楚者，君驕而臣諂也；命無拜而下拜者，君仁而臣敬也。春秋君臣之賢否得失，不亦於此可見乎？雖然，鄭伯逃歸未幾，而有乞盟之舉，則其悔悟深切可知矣；桓公葵丘無何，而有緣陵之專封，則其不能終守臣節可見。噫！鄭文之庸陋，
translation_en: … what is righteous? For King Hui harbored the intention of replacing his heir, whereas Duke Huan held the blood-oath covenant at Shouzhi. Faced with this, a gentleman would surely say: "Prince Zheng is our sovereign's son; moreover, his being the heir apparent was our sovereign's own command. For the feudal lords to covenant at Shouzhi to secure his position is truly the way to honor the royal command and secure the royal heir—how could one be blind to the righteousness of this?" Why then did the Earl of Zheng comply with the private command—"I shall comfort you"—abandon his ceremonial guard, and flee home? He merely knew that a royal command ought to be obeyed, yet was unable to judge whether it was righteous or not. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) not deeply censure him? Thus it is said that obeying a private command without regulating it by righteousness is worthy of ridicule—it is for this reason. As for the Duke of Zhou bearing the royal command to bestow the sacrificial flesh [賜級, 級 for 胙?], and Huan of Qi disobeying the command by descending the steps to bow—how [善何, 善 for 若?] does the Spring and Autumn Annals praise him for being able to regulate his actions by righteousness? For King Xiang extended the grace of kindly nourishing an aged minister, and the Duke of Zhou conveyed the command of commending his toil and bestowing the sacrificial flesh. Faced with this, an ordinary person would surely say: "To descend and bow is ritual propriety; not to descend and bow is the royal command. To obey a favored command and refrain from descending to bow cannot be considered arrogant." Who would be able to regulate this by righteousness? Fortunately, Huan of Qi maintained an awe-inspired reverence before the royal majesty just尺-lengths away, and displayed a briskly respectful demeanor in descending to bow before ascending to receive the gift. He knew only that a minister's integrity must not be compromised, and had no leisure to consider whether the royal command was being disobeyed or not. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals not deeply praise him? Thus it is said that disobeying a favored command while being able to regulate oneself by righteousness is worthy of praise—it is for this reason. Alas! When commanded to follow Chu, to follow Chu shows an arrogant sovereign and a flattering minister; when commanded not to bow, to descend and bow shows a benevolent sovereign and a reverent minister. Can not the worthiness or unworthiness, the successes and failures of sovereigns and ministers in the Spring and Autumn period be seen right here? Even so, not long after the Earl of Zheng fled home, he took the step of begging for a covenant, from which we can know that his remorse and realization were deep and earnest; and not long after Duke Huan's assembly at Kuiqiu, there occurred his unauthorized enfeoffment at Yuanling, from which we can see that he was unable to preserve his ministerial integrity to the end. Alas! The mediocrity and pettiness of Wen of Zheng …

text:

於此可以見伯事之得失矣且夫義者服人心之本
也晉景何為率鄭而不以義耶蓋鄭自戰邲以来反
覆無常非一日矣今也以訟于楚而弗勝歸而請成
于蟲牢鄭之從晉誠可喜矣然當是時天王之訃告
已在諸侯之策使景公能率蟲牢之諸侯以奔國恤
於京師則尊王之義以明而鄭人之心服豈不固乎
夫何景公不明乎此雖王室之訃音久聞而九國之
盟誓不廢晉之服鄭而昧於義如此故鄭人知其終

===
不足以庇己也於是楚始伐鄭而晉救以欒書之兵
患非不施也而鄭人之反覆自如楚再伐鄭而晉援
以四國之師恩非不加也而鄭人之携貳自若揆厥
所自豈非景公義不足以服其心而何愚所謂貳國

之後，晉再救鄭而無功；蕭魚之後，楚再爭鄭而無功，於此可以見伯事之得失矣。
且夫義者，服人心之本也，晉景何為率鄭而不以義耶？蓋鄭自戰邲以来，反覆無常，非一日矣。今也以訟于楚而弗勝，歸而請成于蟲牢，鄭之從晉，誠可喜矣。然當是時，天王之訃告已在諸侯之策，使景公能率蟲牢之諸侯，以奔國恤於京師，則尊王之義以明，而鄭人之心服豈不固乎？夫何景公不明乎此，雖王室之訃音久聞，而九國之盟誓不廢。晉之服鄭而昧於義如此，故鄭人知其終不足以庇己也。於是楚始伐鄭，而晉救以欒書之兵，患非不施也，而鄭人之反覆自如；楚再伐鄭，而晉援以四國之師，恩非不加也，而鄭人之携貳自若。揆厥所自，豈非景公義不足以服其心而何？愚所謂「貳國服而不能示之以義，故恤患之兵徒勤於內」者，以此。
若夫誠者，感人心之機也，晉悼何為服鄭而能以誠耶？蓋鄭自侵蔡以来，服役于楚，非一年矣。今也因晉悼之講會，遂請成于蕭魚，則鄭之服晉，誠可嘉矣。然當是時，晉雖得鄭，安保其不叛耶？使悼公虞其叛復…
translation_en:
…after [the covenant at Chonglao], Jin twice rescued Zheng without success; after [the meeting at] Xiaoyu, Chu twice contended for Zheng without success. From this one can see the successes and failures of hegemonic enterprises.

Moreover, righteousness is the foundation for winning the submission of men's hearts. Why did Duke Jing of Jin (晉景) lead Zheng without using righteousness? Ever since the Battle of Bi (邲), Zheng had been vacillating and inconstant for more than a single day. Now, having lost a dispute in Chu, it returned and requested peace at Chonglao (蟲牢); Zheng's following of Jin was truly cause for joy. Yet at that time, the obituary notice of the Heavenly King was already recorded on the tablets of the feudal lords. Had Duke Jing been able to lead the feudal lords at Chonglao to hasten to the capital for the national mourning, then the righteousness of honoring the King would have been made clear, and how could the heartfelt submission of the people of Zheng not have been firm? Why was it that Duke Jing did not understand this? Although the obituary notice from the royal house had long been heard, the covenant oaths of the nine states were not called off. Because Jin won the submission of Zheng while being so blind to righteousness, the people of Zheng knew that in the end Jin would not be enough to shelter them. Thereupon, when Chu first attacked Zheng and Jin rescued it with the troops of Luan Shu (欒書), it was not that relief in distress [reading 患 as 惠] was not bestowed, yet the people of Zheng remained as vacillating as before; when Chu again attacked Zheng and Jin aided it with the armies of four states, it was not that favor was not extended, yet the people of Zheng remained as duplicitous as ever. Examining where this came from, was it not simply because Duke Jing's righteousness was insufficient to win their hearts? This is the reason for what I meant by "when a vacillating state submits and one cannot show it righteousness, the troops sent to relieve its distress toil in vain within."

As for sincerity, it is themainspring for moving men's hearts. How was it that Duke Dao of Jin (晉悼), in winning the submission of Zheng, was able to do so with sincerity? Ever since its invasion of Cai (蔡), Zheng had submitted to the service of Chu for more than a single year. Now, on account of Duke Dao of Jin's peace conferences, it consequently requested peace at Xiaoyu (蕭魚); Zheng's submission to Jin was truly praiseworthy. Fortunately, Duke Dao had insight into this: he dispensed with the nuisance of covenant oaths and moved them with heartfelt good faith. Because Jin won Zheng's submission and treated them with such sincerity, the people of Zheng knew that in the end Jin could be relied upon. Thereupon, when Chu first applied military force in hopes of winning Zheng's compliance, the Zheng people's devotion to Jin did not waver; when Chu again applied military force in hopes of coercing Zheng into submission, the Zheng people's resolve to turn their backs on Chu grew all the firmer. Considering how his return of the Wenyang lands was insufficient to secure the feudal lords, and his campaign against Jiao was insufficient to command the various states, is he really worth discussing? It is only a pity that although Duke Dao of Jin's winning of Zheng's submission was admirable, afterward, were his establishing relations with the people of Wu at Xiang, and his siding with the subjects of Wei at Qi, also admirable? Alas! If Duke Dao had the qualities of a gentleman and yet his actions were still like this, how can I blame the other hegemons!

人君因時而申明其令既命臣下必斂物以順乎時
復戒臣下無出物以悖乎時夫為治貴乎能順時令
也人君於萬物斂藏之際安得不命臣下務收斂而
勿宣出以順時哉記者謂夫收斂之令王者於孟秋
之月已布之矣今也季秋之月天地之氣已藏其可
===
不申嚴其令乎積蓄之令王者於仲秋之月已布之
矣今也建戌之月萬彙之藏已畢可不申重其命乎
是以百官有司非一職也必命之莫不務收斂諸物
於府庫之內于以合天地閉藏之令焉貴賤上下非
一人也必命之莫不專心積聚百穀於倉廩之中于
以合造化歸藏之義焉彼諸物之當收者深藏之勿

The ruler reiterates and clarifies his ordinances in accordance with the season: having commanded his subjects that they must gather in goods so as to conform to the season, he further warns them not to disburse goods so as to go against the season. Now, in governing, what is valued is the ability to conform to the seasonal ordinances. At the time when the myriad things are being gathered and stored away, how could the ruler not command his subjects to devote themselves to gathering in and not disbursing out, in order to conform to the season? The chronicler says that as for the ordinance on gathering in, the true king had already promulgated it in the first month of autumn; now, in the last month of autumn, when the vital energies of heaven and earth have already been stored away, how could he not reiterate his ordinance with strictness? As for the ordinance on accumulating stores, the true king had already promulgated it in the middle month of autumn; now, in the ninth lunar month (jianxu), when the storing away of all things is already complete, how could he not repeat and emphasize his command? Therefore, the hundred officials and the authorities are not of a single office; he must command that none fail to devote themselves to gathering the various goods inside the treasuries and storehouses, thereby matching the ordinance of heaven and earth's closing and storing away. The noble and the base, superiors and inferiors, are not a single person; he must command that none fail to concentrate on accumulating the hundred grains within the granaries, thereby matching the principle of nature's returning and storing away. Those various goods that ought to be gathered should be deeply stored and not brought out; if one were to open the treasuries and storehouses to disburse them outside, that would go against the seasonal ordinances. The hundred grains that ought to be harvested should be carefully gathered in and not scattered; if one were to open the granaries to distribute them to the people, that would go against the Way of Heaven. Indeed, what was issued forth then was in accordance with the venting and spreading of the yang vital force; what is not brought forth now is in accordance with the gathering and storing of the yin vital force. In the former kings' every gathering in and every issuing forth, what was not in accordance with the seasonal ordinances? This too one must not fail to know.

精不為外物之所二耳不為外物所二則祭之心為
精意精志而無一毫之不誠其精之至也為何如于
以不備樂以為樂不飲酒以為歡所以不樂不歡者
豈故為是虛文耶無非致其德之明不為外物之所
蔽耳不為外物所蔽則祭之道為明禋明享而無纖
芥之不潔其明之至也又何如德既極其精矣由是
奉灌獻而交乎神明則神明雖曰視之弗見今則格
於冥冥之中而如在其上矣曾何神明之不我交乎
德既極其明矣由是具牲幣以事乎鬼神則鬼神雖
===
===
曰聽之不聞今則感於昭昭之際而如在左右矣又
何鬼神之不我接乎是知齊者致誠之道誠者格神
之本記者言此其示人之意深矣抑又論之君子之
祭七日戒三日齊必見所祭者誠之至也是故郊則
天神格廟則人鬼享皆由己以致之也傳曰有其誠
則有其神無其誠則無其神誠之至與不至而神之
感不感係焉有如此可不謹諸

精，不為外物之所二耳。不為外物所二，則祭之心為精意、精志，而無一毫之不誠，其精之至也為何如！于以不備樂以為樂，不飲酒以為歡。所以不樂、不歡者，豈故為是虛文耶？無非致其德之明，不為外物之所蔽耳。不為外物所蔽，則祭之道為明禋、明享，而無纖芥之不潔，其明之至也又何如！德既極其精矣，由是奉灌獻而交乎神明，則神明雖曰視之弗見，今則格於冥冥之中，而如在其上矣，曾何神明之不我交乎？德既極其明矣，由是具牲幣以事乎鬼神，則鬼神雖曰聽之不聞，今則感於昭昭之際，而如在左右矣，又何鬼神之不我接乎？是知齊者，致誠之道；誠者，格神之本。記者言此，其示人之意深矣。抑又論之，君子之祭，七日戒，三日齊，必見所祭者，誠之至也。是故郊則天神格，廟則人鬼享，皆由己以致之也。傳曰：「有其誠則有其神，無其誠則無其神。」誠之至與不至，而神之感不感係焉，有如此，可不謹諸！

translation_en:
…purity, not allowing it to be divided by external things. When it is not divided by external things, the mind in sacrifice becomes one of pure thought and pure intent, without the slightest bit of insincerity—how supreme is such purity! Therefore, one does not prepare music for pleasure, nor drink wine for merriment. Why does one refrain from pleasure and merriment—is it deliberately to make an empty show? It is nothing other than bringing the brightness of one's virtue to the utmost, not allowing it to be obscured by external things. When it is not obscured by external things, the way of sacrifice becomes one of bright libation and bright offering, without the tiniest speck of impurity—and how supreme is such brightness! Once virtue has reached the utmost purity, when one thereby presents libations and offerings to commune with the divine intelligence, then although the divine intelligence is said to be looked for yet unseen, now it approaches in the unseen darkness and is as though present above—how could the divine intelligence ever fail to commune with us? Once virtue has reached the utmost brightness, when one thereby prepares sacrificial victims and silks to serve the ghosts and spirits, then although the ghosts and spirits are said to be listened for yet unheard, now they respond in the bright light and are as though present at one's left and right—how could the ghosts and spirits ever fail to meet with us? Thus we know that fasting is the way to attain sincerity, and sincerity is the foundation for reaching the spirits. In saying this, the recorder of the rites conveyed a profound meaning to instruct people. Furthermore, if we discuss it further: when the noble man sacrifices, he observes seven days of abstinence and three days of strict fasting, so that he surely sees the one to whom he sacrifices; this is the utmost of sincerity. Therefore, in the suburban sacrifice the heavenly spirits approach, and in the ancestral temple the human ghosts enjoy the offerings; all of this is brought about from within oneself. As the commentary says: "Where there is sincerity, there is the spirit; where there is no sincerity, there is no spirit." Since whether the spirits respond or not depends in this way upon whether one's sincerity reaches the utmost or not, how could one not be reverently careful about it!

These are the abuses of popular fashion, and we have suppressed them all. This paper alone is refined and classical in diction, and mature and vigorous in brushwork; therefore, it has been placed in the front ranks.

The discourse states: In a minister's service to his ruler, there is the fundamental and there is the incidental. title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而舍此則無以事其君舍此以事君則功利智
謀之末小人之事君也君子肯以此自處而導
其君於不善之地哉孟子曰君子務引其君以
當道如此戰國之時王道之荆棘也甚矣人心
之榛蕪也極矣在上者惟知功利是圖而不知
道為何事在下者惟知智謀是尚而不知道為
何物故管商之徒引其君以利申韓之徒引其
君以刑孫吳之徒引其君以戰儀秦之徒引其
君以縱横而引君當道者寥寥乎未之見也夫
===
利也刑也戰也縱横也彼孰不以為引君之道
乎由君子觀之乃事君之末耳小人之為耳何
足以言道君子人歟心之所志者此道口之所
談者此道身之所踐履以酬酢乎萬變者此道
故其事君也以責難為恭以陳善閉邪為敬道
莫先於仁君心有未仁也則引之志於仁以立
其體道不外乎義君心有未義也則引之由於
義以達其用聲色貨利戕君心之斧斤也則引
之當道使不邇聲色不殖貨利焉遊田觀逸蠹

義以達其用聲色貨利戕君心之斧斤也則引
之當道使不邇聲色不殖貨利焉遊田觀逸蠱
punctuated: 而舍此，則無以事其君。舍此以事君，則功利智謀之末，小人之事君也。君子肯以此自處，而導其君於不善之地哉？孟子曰：「君子務引其君以當道」，如此。戰國之時，王道之荆棘也甚矣，人心之榛蕪也極矣。在上者惟知功利是圖，而不知道為何事；在下者惟知智謀是尚，而不知道為何物。故管、商之徒引其君以利，申、韓之徒引其君以刑，孫、吳之徒引其君以戰，儀、秦之徒引其君以縱横，而引君當道者，寥寥乎未之見也。夫利也、刑也、戰也、縱横也，彼孰不以為引君之道乎？由君子觀之，乃事君之末耳，小人之為耳，何足以言道！君子人歟，心之所志者此道，口之所談者此道，身之所踐履以酬酢乎萬變者此道。故其事君也，以責難為恭，以陳善閉邪為敬。道莫先於仁，君心有未仁也，則引之志於仁以立其體；道不外乎義，君心有未義也，則引之由於義以達其用。聲色貨利，戕君心之斧斤也，則引之當道，使不邇聲色、不殖貨利焉；遊田觀逸，蠹…
translation_en:
…were to abandon this for a single day, he would have no means to serve his sovereign. To abandon this in serving one's sovereign is to resort to the secondary matters of功利 (utilitarian gain) and clever stratagems—the way petty men serve their sovereign. Would a gentleman willingly place himself in such a position and lead his sovereign into an unwholesome state? This is why Mencius said, "The gentleman makes it his business to guide his sovereign so that he conforms to the Way."

During the Warring States period, the Kingly Way was severely overgrown with brambles, and human minds were utterly choked with weeds. Those above knew only to scheme for utilitarian gain and did not know what the Way was as an enterprise; those below knew only to prize clever stratagems and did not know what the Way was as a reality. Thus, the followers of Guan Zhong and Shang Yang guided their sovereigns by means of profit; the followers of Shen Buhai and Han Fei guided their sovereigns by means of punishments; the followers of Sun Wu and Wu Qi guided their sovereigns by means of warfare; and the followers of Zhang Yi and Su Qin guided their sovereigns by means of vertical and horizontal alliances. Yet those who guided their sovereigns to conform to the Way were nowhere to be seen. Now, as for profit, punishments, warfare, and vertical and horizontal alliances—which of those men did not consider them the way to guide a sovereign? Yet from the viewpoint of the gentleman, these are merely the secondary matters of serving a sovereign, the doings of petty men—how could they be worthy of being called the Way?

The gentleman, however—what his mind aspires to is this Way, what his mouth speaks of is this Way, and what his person puts into practice in responding to a myriad changes is this Way. Therefore, in serving his sovereign, he takes urging difficult achievements upon him as courtesy, and setting forth good while shutting out evil as reverence. In the Way, nothing comes before benevolence; if the sovereign's mind is not yet benevolent, he guides him to set his mind on benevolence so as to establish its substance. The Way is nothing apart from righteousness; if the sovereign's mind is not yet righteous, he guides him to follow righteousness so as to carry out its function. Sensual pleasures and material profit are axes that hack away at the sovereign's mind, so he guides him to conform to the Way, causing him not to draw near to sensual pleasures and not to hoard material profit. Excursions, hunting, sightseeing, and ease are wood-boring…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
君心之蟊賊也則引之當道使罔淫于觀于逸
于遊于田焉君未恭儉也引之以恭儉而恭儉
非道乎君未學問也引之以學問而學問非道
乎君未納諫也引之以納諫而納諫非道乎君
未愛民引之以愛民君未用賢引之以用賢而
愛民也用賢也又非道乎以堯舜之道引其君
君不堯舜不止也以文武之道引其君君不文
武不止也君子之事君如此國未富也非所憂
兵未強也非所憂法令未行也非所憂諸侯未
===
服也非所憂而所憂者惟恐吾君之未至於道
耳蓋吾君所存念念乎道吾君所行事事乎道
則心以正身以修家以齊國以治紀綱以立制
度以明禮樂以興教化以行而天下自平無事
乎利而國自富矣無事乎戰而兵自強矣無事
乎刑而民自化矣無事乎縱橫而諸侯自服矣
雖不求利而自無不利是何也由吾之所以事
君者以其本耳視彼小人汲汲以功利智謀事
其君其心惟欲富其國而已強其兵而已威乎

punctuated: 君心之蟊賊也，則引之當道，使罔淫于觀、于逸、于遊、于田焉。君未恭儉也，引之以恭儉，而恭儉非道乎？君未學問也，引之以學問，而學問非道乎？君未納諫也，引之以納諫，而納諫非道乎？君未愛民，引之以愛民；君未用賢，引之以用賢，而愛民也、用賢也，又非道乎？以堯、舜之道引其君，君不堯、舜不止也；以文、武之道引其君，君不文、武不止也。君子之事君如此。國未富也，非所憂；兵未強也，非所憂；法令未行也，非所憂；諸侯未服也，非所憂；而所憂者，惟恐吾君之未至於道耳。蓋吾君所存，念念乎道；吾君所行，事事乎道，則心以正，身以修，家以齊，國以治，紀綱以立，制度以明，禮樂以興，教化以行，而天下自平。無事乎利而國自富矣，無事乎戰而兵自強矣，無事乎刑而民自化矣，無事乎縱橫而諸侯自服矣。雖不求利，而自無不利。是何也？由吾之所以事君者以其本耳。視彼小人，汲汲以功利智謀事其君，其心惟欲富其國而已，強其兵而已，威乎
translation_en: …are pests that eat away at the ruler's mind, so he guides him onto the right Way, ensuring that he does not indulge excessively in sightseeing, ease, excursions, or hunting. If the ruler is not yet reverent and frugal, he guides him with reverence and frugality—and are not reverence and frugality the Way? If the ruler does not yet engage in learning and inquiry, he guides him with learning and inquiry—and are not learning and inquiry the Way? If the ruler does not yet accept remonstrance, he guides him to accept remonstrance—and is not accepting remonstrance the Way? If the ruler does not yet love the people, he guides him to love the people; if the ruler does not yet employ the worthy, he guides him to employ the worthy—and are not loving the people and employing the worthy also the Way? Guiding his ruler with the Way of Yao and Shun, he does not stop until his ruler becomes like Yao and Shun; guiding his ruler with the Way of King Wen and King Wu, he does not stop until his ruler becomes like Wen and Wu. Such is how the noble man serves his ruler. That the state is not yet wealthy is not what he worries about; that the army is not yet strong is not what he worries about; that laws and ordinances are not yet enforced is not what he worries about; that the feudal lords have not yet submitted is not what he worries about. What he worries about is solely the fear that his ruler has not yet attained the Way. For when what our ruler preserves in his heart is, in every thought, the Way, and what our ruler practices is, in every deed, the Way, then his mind is rectified, his person is cultivated, his family is regulated, his state is rightly governed, fundamental principles are established, institutions are clarified, rites and music flourish, moral transformation is carried out, and the world is naturally brought to peace. Without busying oneself with profit, the state naturally becomes wealthy; without busying oneself with warfare, the army naturally becomes strong; without busying oneself with punishments, the people are naturally transformed; without busying oneself with strategic alliances, the feudal lords naturally submit. Even though one does not seek profit, there is naturally nothing that is not profitable. Why is this? It is simply because the means by which I serve the ruler is through the root. Look at those petty men who anxiously serve their ruler with utilitarian achievements and clever schemes: in their minds they desire only to enrich his state, to strengthen his army, to overawe…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
民而已服乎諸侯而已殊不知所欲未得而害
已隨之是何也徒知事君之末而不知吾君子
之道故也是知君子事君以其本故君德益盛
而獲莫大之福小人事君以其末故君欲益熾
而致無窮之禍此君子所以善於事君而大有
益於國家夫豈小人所可同年語哉孟軻氏以
此為慎子告其曉之之意深矣惜乎慎子不足
以語此我思古人伊尹以堯舜之道引湯而湯
為堯舜之君周公以文武之道引成王而成王
===
為文武之君夫以湯之聖成王之賢而所以成
其德者不能不有資於伊周大臣如此方今
聖天子在上聰明睿智文武聖神德已盛矣道已至
矣化已成矣然而賛襄密勿補
袞職萬一之闕者能不有望於今日大臣
又
王鏊

punctuated:
民而已，服乎諸侯而已。殊不知所欲未得，而害已隨之。是何也？徒知事君之末，而不知吾君子之道故也。是知君子事君以其本，故君德益盛而獲莫大之福；小人事君以其末，故君欲益熾而致無窮之禍。此君子所以善於事君，而大有益於國家，夫豈小人所可同年語哉！孟軻氏以此為慎子告，其曉之之意深矣，惜乎慎子不足以語此。我思古人，伊尹以堯、舜之道引湯，而湯為堯、舜之君；周公以文、武之道引成王，而成王為文、武之君。夫以湯之聖、成王之賢，而所以成其德者，不能不有資於伊、周大臣如此。方今聖天子在上，聰明睿智，文武聖神，德已盛矣，道已至矣，化已成矣。然而賛襄密勿、補袞職萬一之闕者，能不有望於今日大臣！

又
王鏊

translation_en:
… the people, and to subjugate the feudal lords. Little do they realize that before what they desire is even obtained, harm already follows upon its heels. Why is this? It is because they know only the superficialities of serving a ruler, and do not know the Way of us noble men. Thus we know that when a noble man serves his ruler, he does so through the fundamentals, and therefore the ruler's virtue flourishes ever more and he reaps the greatest of blessings; when a petty man serves his ruler, he does so through superficialities, and therefore the ruler's desires blaze ever more fiercely and he brings about endless calamities. This is why the noble man excels at serving his ruler and brings great benefit to the state—how could the petty man be spoken of in the same breath! When Mencius (Meng Ke 孟軻) told this to Shenzi 慎子, his intention to enlighten him was profound indeed; alas, Shenzi was not worthy of conversing on such matters. I think of the ancients: Yi Yin 伊尹 guided Tang 湯 with the Way of Yao 堯 and Shun 舜, and Tang became a ruler like Yao and Shun; the Duke of Zhou 周公 guided King Cheng 成王 with the Way of Kings Wen 文 and Wu 武, and King Cheng became a ruler like Wen and Wu. Even with the sageliness of Tang and the worthiness of King Cheng, that by which they perfected their virtue could not but rely on great ministers like Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou to such an extent. At present, the Sacred Son of Heaven reigns above, discerning and wise, civil and martial, sagely and divine; his virtue is already flourishing, his Way is already perfected, and his transformative influence is already accomplished. Yet in assisting him with diligence in confidential affairs and mending even a ten-thousandth of a lapse in the imperial duties, how can one not place hope in the great ministers of today!

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
知為古器也
同考試官學正胡批此篇說出人臣事君之道
議論層出而文勢滔滔如長江大河奔放盪激浩
乎莫之能禦傑作也
考試官修撰鄭批論場非無豐贍葩藻之作
然皆時文耳晚得此卷文詞竒古議論激烈而英
氣崢嶸盖駸駸乎古作者烏可目之為科場文耶
故不厭其重而錄之
考試官左諭德謝批通篇議論皆自胷中流出
===
而詞嚴誼正足見平日抱負予於初場之夕盖嘗
夢得竒士矣非子其誰
人臣事君之法其始也必有一定之志而其後
也必有一定之守志定於先則必以道望其君
而霸功異術不能惑守定於後則必以道正其
君而毁譽得失不能移而所以堯舜其君者在
是矣志不立則將以術為道守不定則將以道
徇君而何以引其君於當道哉故志有立於先
守無變於後而必以道者此萬世事君之法也

人臣事君之法，其始也必有一定之志，而其後也必有一定之守。志定於先，則必以道望其君，而霸功異術不能惑；守定於後，則必以道正其君，而毁譽得失不能移。而所以堯、舜其君者，在是矣。志不立，則將以術為道；守不定，則將以道徇君。而何以引其君於當道哉？故志有立於先，守無變於後，而必以道者，此萬世事君之法也，

Associate Examiner Hu, Director of Studies (xuezheng), comments: This piece articulates the Way by which a minister serves his ruler. Its arguments emerge layer upon layer, and its literary momentum surges on and on like the Yangtze and Yellow rivers—rushing forth and churning with force, so vast that nothing can withstand it. It is a masterpiece.
Examiner Zheng, Senior Compiler (xiuzhuan), comments: In the discourse session there was no lack of richly abundant and ornate compositions, yet all of them were merely contemporary examination prose. Late in the reading I came upon this paper: its diction is strikingly archaic, its arguments impassioned, and its heroic spirit towering. Indeed, it presses close upon the writers of antiquity—how could one regard it merely as an examination-hall essay? Therefore, without minding the duplication, we have selected it for inclusion.
Examiner Xie, Left Admonisher (zuo yude), comments: The arguments throughout the entire piece all flow straight from his breast, and the diction is stern and the principles upright, quite sufficient to show his everyday aspirations. On the evening of the first session, I in fact dreamed of obtaining an extraordinary scholar—if not you, who else could it be?

In the method by which a minister serves his ruler, at the beginning he must have a fixed resolve, and afterward he must have a fixed steadfastness. When his resolve is fixed beforehand, he will certainly look to his ruler in accordance with the Way, and hegemonic achievements or heterodox arts cannot delude him; when his steadfastness is fixed afterward, he will certainly rectify his ruler in accordance with the Way, and praise or blame, gain or loss, cannot move him. Herein lies the means by which to make one's ruler a Yao or a Shun. If his resolve is not established, he will take mere statecraft to be the Way; if his steadfastness is not fixed, he will bend the Way to accommodate his ruler. How then could he guide his ruler onto the proper Way? Therefore, having resolve established beforehand, having steadfastness unchanged afterward, and unfailingly acting in accordance with the Way—this is the method for serving one's ruler for ten thousand generations,…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
亦萬世臣子之心也孟子曰君子之事君也務
引其君以當道是心也愛君者知之有志者知
之有守者知之彼慎子者何足以知此古之人
有欲其君王者矣有欲其君霸者矣有欲其君
強者矣志固各有在也以強者務引之強而止
欲進而霸不可得也以霸者務引之霸而止欲
進而王不可得也君子所務則異於是其存也
有所本其發也有所歸其講貫於平昔也有所
得其蘊蓄於胷中也有其具其經綸也何道其
===
調燮也何為其寅亮也何說蓋必有定志矣此
志一定恪守不移逆鱗可批而此志不可渝也
鼎鑊可蹈而此志不可奪也務引之道而止蓋
君子之愛君也深故其憂君也至其憂君也至
故其告君也切誠以天下之本在於一人一人
之主在於一心人君於深宮淵默之際發一念
而正焉則天下蒙其福發一念而雜焉則天下
受其害為之臣者得不以為憂耶是故不待其
發於政而後諫也不待其萌於心而後諫也未

punctuated: 亦萬世臣子之心也。孟子曰：「君子之事君也，務引其君以當道。」是心也，愛君者知之，有志者知之，有守者知之。彼慎子者，何足以知此？古之人，有欲其君王者矣，有欲其君霸者矣，有欲其君強者矣，志固各有在也。以強者務引之強而止，欲進而霸不可得也；以霸者務引之霸而止，欲進而王不可得也。君子所務則異於是：其存也有所本，其發也有所歸；其講貫於平昔也有所得，其蘊蓄於胷中也有其具。其經綸也何道？其調燮也何為？其寅亮也何說？蓋必有定志矣。此志一定，恪守不移；逆鱗可批，而此志不可渝也；鼎鑊可蹈，而此志不可奪也。務引之道而止。蓋君子之愛君也深，故其憂君也至；其憂君也至，故其告君也切。誠以天下之本在於一人，一人之主在於一心。人君於深宮淵默之際，發一念而正焉，則天下蒙其福；發一念而雜焉，則天下受其害。為之臣者，得不以為憂耶？是故不待其發於政而後諫也，不待其萌於心而後諫也，未
translation_en: … and it is also the heart-mind of ministers and sons for ten thousand generations. Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) said: "When the noble man serves his ruler, he strives solely to guide his ruler onto the rightful Way." This heart-mind is known to those who love their ruler, known to those who possess resolve, and known to those who maintain firm adherence. As for someone like Master Shen (Shenzi 慎子), how could he be worthy of knowing this? Among the ancients, there were those who wished their ruler to be a true king, those who wished their ruler to be a hegemon, and those who wished their ruler merely to be strong; their resolves naturally each had their own focus. Those aiming at strength strove to guide their ruler to strength and stopped there, so even if one wished to advance further to hegemony, it could not be achieved; those aiming at hegemony strove to guide their ruler to hegemony and stopped there, so even if one wished to advance further to true kingship, it could not be achieved. What the noble man strives for, however, differs from this: what he preserves within has a foundation, and what he puts forth has a proper destination; what he has studied and mastered in ordinary times has yielded true understanding, and what he has stored up in his breast provides the necessary wherewithal. By what Way does he order the state? Through what action does he harmonize the cosmos? By what doctrine does he reverently brighten the realm? Surely, he must have a fixed resolve. Once this resolve is fixed, he adheres to it reverently and unswervingly: the dragon's reversed scales may be brushed against, yet this resolve cannot be altered; the boiling cauldron may be trodden into, yet this resolve cannot be wrested away. He strives to guide the ruler onto the Way and stops at nothing less. For when the noble man's love for his ruler is deep, his concern for his ruler is utmost; and because his concern for his ruler is utmost, his counsel to his ruler is earnest. Truly, this is because the foundation of the realm lies in the One Man, and the master of the One Man lies in his single heart-mind. When the ruler is in the deep palace in profound silence, if he gives rise to a single thought that is upright, the entire realm receives its blessing; if he gives rise to a single thought that is impure, the entire realm suffers its harm. How could one who serves as his minister not take this as a cause for anxiety? title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
萌而導焉務欲其天理之常存既發而導焉務
欲其人欲之盡去人曰太平矣而君子常若有
厝薪之憂人曰聖神矣而君子猶或以桓靈為
喻其憂君之心盖無時而不存也進而思曰吾
何以正君退而思曰吾何以正君左納言亦思
曰吾何以正君右納言亦思曰吾何以正君端
士輔君心者也吾則引之以親賢臣憸人蠹君
心者也吾則引之以遠小人學問養君心者也
吾則引之以經史奢侈誘君心者也吾則引之
===
以節儉論道德必稱堯舜引之於堯舜也論征
伐必稱湯武引之於湯武也論好貨也引之於
公劉論好色也引之於太王好兵也引之於干
羽兩階好田也引之於車攻吉日君曰是臣曰
非君曰可臣曰不可所謂直諫直諫引之於道
也君曰是臣亦曰是君曰非臣亦曰非所謂諷
諫諷諫亦引之於道也左而左導焉右而右導
焉無一念而不以正君為務者是豈有所為而
為耶抑豈有所畏而不為耶有為而為則可以

translation_en: …before it has even sprouted, he guides him, striving to ensure that Heavenly Principle is constantly preserved; once it has been expressed, he guides him, striving to ensure that human desires are completely eliminated. Others say, "All is in great peace!" yet the superior man constantly harbors a concern as if resting on a pile of kindling; others say, "He is sagely and神-like!" yet the superior man may still use Emperors Huan (桓) and Ling (靈) of Han as cautionary examples. His heart that worries for his ruler is indeed present at every moment. When advancing to court, he reflects, "How shall I rectify my ruler?" When retiring from court, he reflects, "How shall I rectify my ruler?" Presenting counsel on the left, he likewise reflects, "How shall I rectify my ruler?" Presenting counsel on the right, he likewise reflects, "How shall I rectify my ruler?" Upright scholars are those who assist the ruler's mind, so I lead him to draw close to worthy ministers; flatterers are those who corrode the ruler's mind, so I lead him to keep petty men at a distance; learning and inquiry are what nourish the ruler's mind, so I lead him to the Classics and Histories; extravagance is what seduces the ruler's mind, so I lead him to frugality. In discussing morality and virtue, he invariably cites Yao (堯) and Shun (舜), leading him toward Yao and Shun; in discussing punitive expeditions, he invariably cites Tang (湯) and Wu (武), leading him toward Tang and Wu; in discussing a fondness for wealth, he leads him to Duke Liu (Gong Liu 公劉); in discussing a fondness for beauty, he leads him to King Tai (Tai Wang 太王); if he is fond of warfare, he leads him to the shields and feathers danced between the two staircases; if he is fond of hunting, he leads him to the odes "Sturdy Chariots" (Che gong 車攻) and "Auspicious Day" (Ji ri 吉日). When the ruler says "Right" and the minister says "Wrong," or the ruler says "Permissible" and the minister says "Impermissible"—this is what is called direct remonstrance, and direct remonstrance leads him to the Way. When the ruler says "Right" and the minister also says "Right," or the ruler says "Wrong" and the minister also says "Wrong"—this is what is called indirect remonstrance, and indirect remonstrance likewise leads him to the Way. Turning left, he guides him on the left; turning right, he guides him on the right—there is not a single thought that does not take rectifying the ruler as its urgent duty. title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
利誘也君子祿之以萬鍾有不受有畏而不為
則可以威警也君子怵之以斧鉞有不懼其或
不從雖引裾可也其又不從雖折檻可也其又
不從雖碎首玉階可也是非好名也是非矯激
也誠愛吾君之心之無已也若夫君未有好也
而以南威之色儀狄之酒啟之君未有欲也而
以上林之侈長楊之獵啟之天旱則啟之曰意
乾封乎霖雨則啟之曰不害農也德如堯舜矣
何為不樂世已太平矣何欲不遂若是者惟小
===
人能之君子不能也疇昔所志何若所守何在
而乃如此乎伊周所以引君者尚矣彼多欲之
砭汲長孺所以引武帝也而有淮陽之行佛骨
之諫韓昌黎所以引憲宗也而有潮陽之貶愚
以是知引君者固臣之義而納諫者尤君之明
蓋小人之事君順其欲者也君子之事君拂其
欲者也順其欲者似愛君拂其欲者似忤旨而
天下之治忽實於是乎分君天下者尚鑒茲哉

利誘也，君子祿之以萬鍾有不受；有畏而不為，則可以威警也，君子怵之以斧鉞有不懼。其或不從，雖引裾可也；其又不從，雖折檻可也；其又不從，雖碎首玉階可也。是非好名也，是非矯激也，誠愛吾君之心之無已也。若夫君未有好也，而以南威之色、儀狄之酒啟之；君未有欲也，而以上林之侈、長楊之獵啟之；天旱則啟之曰：「意乾封乎？」霖雨則啟之曰：「不害農也。」德如堯、舜矣，何為不樂？世已太平矣，何欲不遂？若是者，惟小人能之，君子不能也。疇昔所志何若？所守何在？而乃如此乎！伊、周所以引君者尚矣。彼多欲之砭，汲長孺所以引武帝也，而有淮陽之行；佛骨之諫，韓昌黎所以引憲宗也，而有潮陽之貶。愚以是知引君者固臣之義，而納諫者尤君之明。蓋小人之事君，順其欲者也；君子之事君，拂其欲者也。順其欲者似愛君，拂其欲者似忤旨，而天下之治忽實於是乎分。君天下者，尚鑒茲哉！

translation_en:
… be enticed by profit, yet a gentleman might decline even a stipend of ten thousand measures of grain; if he refrained from acting out of fear, then he could be intimidated by force, yet a gentleman will not be frightened even when threatened with the executioner's axe. Should the ruler not heed him, even tugging at the hem of his robe is permissible; should he still not heed him, even breaking the palace balustrade is permissible; should he still not heed him, even dashing one's head against the jade steps is permissible. This is not out of a fondness for fame, nor is it out of perverse extremity; it is truly because the heart that loves one's ruler knows no bounds. As for cases where the ruler does not yet have a fondness, and someone tempts him with the beauty of Nan Wei or the wine of Yi Di; where the ruler does not yet have a desire, and someone tempts him with the extravagance of the Shanglin Park or the hunts at the Changyang Palace; when there is a drought, tempting him by saying, "Perhaps Heaven intends a dry Feng sacrifice?" and when there are torrential rains, tempting him by saying, "It does not harm agriculture"; saying, "Your virtue already equals that of Yao and Shun, why not take pleasure? The world is already in great peace, what desire should go unfulfilled?"—such things only a petty man can do; a gentleman cannot do them. What were his past aspirations like? Where are the principles he held fast to? How could he act like this! The ways in which Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou guided their rulers are of the highest antiquity. That pointed critique regarding "many desires" was how Ji Changru (Ji An 汲黯) guided Emperor Wu of Han, yet it resulted in his reassignment to Huaiyang; the remonstrance concerning the Buddha's bone was how Han Changli (Han Yu 韓愈) guided Emperor Xianzong of Tang, yet it resulted in his banishment to Chaoyang. From this I know that while guiding the ruler is assuredly the duty of the minister, accepting remonstrance is even more the mark of an enlightened ruler. For when a petty man serves his ruler, he indulges his desires; when a gentleman serves his ruler, he thwarts his desires. He who indulges his desires seems to love the ruler, while he who thwarts his desires seems to defy the imperial will; yet the order or ruin of the realm truly parts ways right here. May those who rule over the realm take this as a mirror!

Memorial (Biao)

translation_en:
A Memorial Imitating Song Statesman Sima Guang 司馬光 Expressing Gratitude for the Bestowal of the Imperial Preface to the Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (Zizhi tongjian xu 資治通鑑序)

By He Jun 賀俊

Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor Zheng 鄭: The memorial is grounded in historical fact and is well worth reading.
Comment by Examiner, Senior Compiler Zheng 鄭: Classically elegant.
Comment by Examiner, Left Admonisher Xie 謝: Captures the style of a Song-dynasty memorial.

I humbly submit: Modeling a chronological history upon the History of the Unicorn (Spring and Autumn Annals) to serve as an aid to the mirror of the Ninefold Palace; illuminating imperial compositions to confer special favor and thereby manifest glory for a hundred generations—this is indeed the ultimate honor for a Confucian scholar and truly a grand occasion for this culture of ours.

I humbly reflect that your servant Guang is dull and obtuse by nature and understanding, and barren and superficial in scholarship and learning. Having roughly perused the books from the Spring and Autumn period onward, I exhaustively investigated the traces of order and disorder, rise and fall. Sighing over their prolixity, I extracted the essentials and committed them to bamboo slips [? text appears to drop characters in the parallel couplet here]; yet considering that with my meager strength it was difficult to complete, my hair was soon about to turn white.

I humbly encountered the Late Emperor, who attended to governance with thoughts of order, examined antiquity, and esteemed culture. He commanded me to compile a new work, allowing me to fulfill my original aspiration. Books were lent from the Three Institutes, and writing brushes and tablets were supplied from the Directorate for Imperial Manufactories. Bestowals and rewards were repeatedly conferred, such as few among your servant's colleagues have ever attained.

Reverently I reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor rises daily in sagely reverence, endowed by Heaven with keen intelligence. Reverently upholding the great mandate, You succeed to the vast foundation of the One Ancestor and Four Progenitors; grandly unfolding the imperial plan, You bring about the flourishing governance of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. text:
輯成編輒封進
覽上下蒐羅千三百載之事出入將隨十有九年
之勞少攄一得之愚仰副
兩朝之命第撰次無法抵牾多端方將待罪
闕庭詎意蒙
恩褒飾
詔經筵以進講揮
宸翰以賜名茲又序其本原弁諸篇帙焜煌有耀

===
上繼商周之訓誥下陋漢唐之詠歌典刑總會
之褒冊牘淵林之譽榮踰華袞臣實汗顏彼馬
遷史才揚芳百祀董狐直筆獨步千秋皆未嘗
親屈
鴻藻曲賜揄揚如臣今日之榮者也遂使螢爝之
照依
日月而長明草木之微附
天地而不朽
寵光優渥喜愧交并伏願

punctuated: 輯成編，輒封進覽。上下蒐羅，千三百載之事；出入將隨，十有九年之勞。少攄一得之愚，仰副兩朝之命。第撰次無法，抵牾多端，方將待罪闕庭，詎意蒙恩褒飾：詔經筵以進講，揮宸翰以賜名。茲又序其本原，弁諸篇帙。焜煌有耀，如奎璧之麗層霄；渾噩無涯，若江漢之行大地。上繼商、周之訓誥，下陋漢、唐之詠歌。典刑總會之褒，冊牘淵林之譽，榮踰華袞，臣實汗顏。彼馬遷史才，揚芳百祀；董狐直筆，獨步千秋，皆未嘗親屈鴻藻，曲賜揄揚，如臣今日之榮者也。遂使螢爝之照，依日月而長明；草木之微，附天地而不朽。寵光優渥，喜愧交并。伏願
translation_en: …having compiled it into a finished work, I forthwith sealed and presented it for Your Majesty's perusal. Searching above and below, it encompasses the events of one thousand three hundred years; attending upon it at home and abroad, it represents the labor of nineteen years. I have modestly set forth my humble understanding in order to fulfill with reverence the commands of two reigns. Yet my arrangement lacks method and contains manifold inconsistencies; just as I was awaiting punishment at the palace court, how could I have expected to receive the favor of Your generous praise: ordering that it be lectured upon at the Classics Colloquium, and wielding the imperial brush to bestow upon it a title! Now You have further written a preface explaining its origins to stand at the head of its volumes. Resplendent and radiant, it is like the constellations Kui and Bi adorning the highest heavens; profound, majestic, and boundless, it is like the Yangtze and Han rivers coursing across the great earth. Above, it continues the Instructions and Announcements of the Shang and Zhou; below, it makes the songs and verses of the Han and Tang seem mean by comparison. The praise of it as a "compendium of canonical models" and the commendation of it as a "deep forest of records and documents" are an honor surpassing the華袞 ceremonial robes, making Your servant truly blush with shame. Even Sima Qian (馬遷), whose talent as a historian spread its fragrance for a hundred generations, and Dong Hu (董狐), whose upright brush stood unrivalled for a thousand autumns, never experienced the sovereign personally condescending to compose grand literary prose and graciously bestowing praise upon them, such as the glory Your servant enjoys today. Thus is the faint glow of a firefly or torch enabled to shine forever by relying upon the sun and moon, and the insignificance of grass and trees made imperishable by attaching itself to Heaven and Earth. Your favor and grace are abundant and rich; joy and shame mingle within me. I humbly pray that…

translation_en:
…reflect upon the rise and fall of former dynasties, and examine the successes and failures of the present day; rest in where You should rest in order to bring peace to the common people, and rectify the imperial court in order to rectify the hundred officials. May ten thousand blessings gather together, securing the Imperial dominion upon bedrock; with three acclamations of "Long Live the Emperor," Your servant offers prayers, wishing that Your Sacred longevity may equal Heaven. Your servant, overwhelmed to the utmost with looking up to Heaven and gazing toward the Sage in earnest gratitude and fearful reverence, respectfully presents this memorial of thanks for Your Majesty's hearing.

Third Session
Policy Essays
First Question
Wang Ao 王鏊

Associate Examiner and Instructor Yuan 原 comments: He skillfully answers all five questions; his literary expression is surging and abundant, and his presentation of facts is clear and plain. His essay on current affairs especially shows decisive judgment. He is truly a master of the policy essay, and it is fitting that he be placed first among the many scholars.

Associate Examiner and Subprefectural Instructor Hu 胡 comments: Setting forth the five policy essays item by item, his command of the facts is verified and detailed. None could do this without being steeped in the Classics and Histories and possessing insight into current affairs. He is completely worthy of being recommended for first place.

Associate Examiner and Prefectural Instructor Lin 林 comments: In the policy session, examination candidates are mostly… [troubled] by factual matters and current affairs…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
所窘惟此五篇考究詳明處置得當敻異衆作其
崐山片玉桂林一枝歟可嘉可嘉
考試官修撰鄭批五策條答無遺不為問目
所制其積學有素之士乎良金美玉自有定價擢
冠秋闈宜矣明春南宫之捷
大廷之對裒然出色者予端有望於子
考試官左諭德謝批該博之學政事之才昌大
之氣於五策發之得士如此自信可少副
朝廷之簡命矣他日效用范文正之功業幸毋負此志
===
聖人作之君而賞善罰惡之令行
聖人作之師而勸善懲惡之典著盖權賞罰以治天
下者君道之當然也示勸懲以化天下者師道
之當然也
聖人盡君師之道如此為人臣者可不勉其善戒其
惡以弼成一代治化之盛哉昔我
宣宗章皇帝以聖人之德在
天子之位賞罰之令既行乎一時乃於
萬幾之暇采輯東周以降人臣善可為法惡可為

所窘，惟此五篇考究詳明，處置得當，敻異衆作。其崐山片玉、桂林一枝歟？可嘉，可嘉！
考試官修撰鄭批：五策條答無遺，不為問目所制，其積學有素之士乎！良金美玉自有定價，擢冠秋闈宜矣。明春南宫之捷、大廷之對，裒然出色者，予端有望於子。
考試官左諭德謝批：該博之學、政事之才、昌大之氣，於五策發之。得士如此，自信可少副朝廷之簡命矣。他日效用，范文正之功業，幸毋負此志。
聖人作之君，而賞善罰惡之令行；聖人作之師，而勸善懲惡之典著。盖權賞罰以治天下者，君道之當然也；示勸懲以化天下者，師道之當然也。聖人盡君師之道如此，為人臣者，可不勉其善、戒其惡，以弼成一代治化之盛哉！昔我宣宗章皇帝以聖人之德，在天子之位，賞罰之令既行乎一時，乃於萬幾之暇，采輯東周以降人臣善可為法、惡可為
translation_en:
…stymied by [matters of historical fact and current affairs]; only these five essays investigate things thoroughly and clearly and handle them appropriately, standing far apart from the compositions of the crowd. Is this not a shard of jade from Mount Kun, a single branch from the cassia forest? Praiseworthy, truly praiseworthy!

Examiner and Senior Compiler Zheng comments: The five policy essays answer every point without omission and are not constrained by the questions posed. Truly a scholar of long-accumulated learning! Fine gold and beautiful jade naturally have a set value; it is fitting that he be selected to top the autumn examination. In next spring's triumph at the Southern Palace [Metropolitan Examination] and response in the Great Court [Palace Examination], I truly have high hopes that you will stand out preeminently.

Examiner and Left Admonisher Xie comments: Comprehensive learning, talent for governance, and a grand, flourishing vigor are all expressed in these five policy essays. In obtaining a scholar such as this, I feel confident that I have gone some small way toward fulfilling the Court's commission. When you render service in days to come, pray do not betray this aspiration toward the achievements of Fan Wenzheng [Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹].

When the Sage acts as their Ruler, commands that reward the good and punish the evil are put into effect; when the Sage acts as their Teacher, canons that encourage the good and chastise the evil are made manifest. For weighing rewards and punishments in order to govern All under Heaven is the natural duty of the Way of the Ruler; displaying encouragement and warning in order to transform All under Heaven is the natural duty of the Way of the Teacher. Since the Sage fulfills the Way of Ruler and Teacher to such a degree, how could those who serve as ministers not strive after what is good and guard against what is evil, so as to assist in accomplishing the flourishing governance and transformation of an entire era! In former times, Our Emperor Xuanzong Zhang [the Xuande Emperor, r. 1425–1435], possessing the virtue of a sage and occupying the position of Son of Heaven, having already put commands of reward and punishment into effect in his own time, thereupon in his leisure from a myriad affairs of state compiled from the Eastern Zhou onward instances of ministers whose goodness could serve as a model and whose evil could serve as…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
戒者類為臣鑒一書頒示群臣俾時省覽其有
益於臣工信大矣愚嘗拜手稽首莊誦
聖訓而嘆曰大哉
皇言乎其即成湯告諸侯以各守爾典無即慆淫之
語乎其即成王訓百官以恭儉惟德無載爾偽
之義乎
宸翰汪洋未易備舉姑因明問所及而陳之如祭
遵之憂國奉公而興光武安得之思韓休之守
正不阿而啓玄宗安寢之嘆舟中惟圖書衣衾
===
而江南幹事以回曹武穆之清慎為第一名將
可敬也胷中有數萬甲兵而西夏聞之膽破范
文正之功業為第一流人物可慕也臣鑒載此
豈非欲為臣者讀之為祭為韓為曹為范歟張
湯之深文舞知而致海內之騷動李林甫之口
蜜腹劍而致胡雛之倡逆謬為豐亨豫大之說
而視官爵財物之棄如糞土蔡京啓君侈心之
罪可誅也倡有天書雲篆之符而致神霄玉清
之祠遍天下蔡攸引君異端之罪可戮也臣鑒

punctuated: 戒者，類為《臣鑒》一書，頒示群臣，俾時省覽，其有益於臣工，信大矣！愚嘗拜手稽首，莊誦聖訓，而嘆曰：「大哉皇言乎！其即成湯告諸侯以『各守爾典，無即慆淫』之語乎？其即成王訓百官以『恭儉惟德，無載爾偽』之義乎？」宸翰汪洋，未易備舉，姑因明問所及而陳之。如祭遵之憂國奉公，而興光武安得之思；韓休之守正不阿，而啓玄宗安寢之嘆。舟中惟圖書衣衾，而江南幹事以回，曹武穆之清慎為第一名將，可敬也；胷中有數萬甲兵，而西夏聞之膽破，范文正之功業為第一流人物，可慕也。《臣鑒》載此，豈非欲為臣者讀之，為祭、為韓、為曹、為范歟？張湯之深文舞知，而致海內之騷動；李林甫之口蜜腹劍，而致胡雛之倡逆。謬為豐亨豫大之說，而視官爵財物之棄如糞土，蔡京啓君侈心之罪可誅也；倡有天書雲篆之符，而致神霄玉清之祠遍天下，蔡攸引君異端之罪可戮也。《臣鑒》
translation_en:
…serve as a warning, categorizing them into the book Mirror for Ministers (Chenjian) and distributing it to all the officials so that they might examine and peruse it from time to time. Its benefit to the officials is truly great! I have bowed my head to the hands and knocked my head on the ground, solemnly reciting the Sacred Instructions, and sighed: "Great indeed are the august words! Are they not the very words with which Tang the Successful admonished the feudal lords: 'Each of you observe your statutes, and do not give yourselves over to insolence and excess'? Are they not the very meaning with which King Cheng instructed the hundred officials: 'Be reverent and frugal in virtue, and do not harbor falsehood'?"

The imperial writings are vast as an ocean and not easy to enumerate in full, so for now I shall set them forth in accordance with what the sagacious question has touched upon. For instance, Zhai Zun 祭遵 worried for the state and devoted himself to the public good, thereby inspiring Emperor Guangwu's longing for how such men could be obtained; Han Xiu 韓休 upheld rectitude without flattery, thereby prompting Emperor Xuanzong's sigh about sleeping in peace. Having only books, charts, clothes, and quilts in his boat when returning from accomplishing his mission in Jiangnan—the integrity and prudence of Cao Wumu 曹武穆 [Cao Bin 曹彬] made him the foremost famous general, worthy of reverence; having tens of thousands of armored soldiers in his breast so that Western Xia's courage broke upon hearing of him—the meritorious achievements of Fan Wenzheng 范文正 [Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹] made him a figure of the very first rank, worthy of admiration. That the Mirror for Ministers records these men—is it not because it desires that those who serve as ministers, upon reading it, should become like Zhai, Han, Cao, and Fan?

Zhang Tang 張湯 manipulated the letter of the law with cunning, bringing about turmoil within the seas; Li Linfu 李林甫 had honey on his lips and a sword in his belly, bringing about the rebellion initiated by the barbarian whelp [An Lushan 安祿山]. Falsely promoting the doctrine of abundance, prosperity, ease, and greatness, and regarding the squandering of official ranks and wealth like dirt and dung—Cai Jing's 蔡京 crime of arousing the ruler's extravagant desires deserves death; fabricating talismans of heavenly books and cloud-seal script, and causing shrines of Shenxiao and Yuqing to fill the realm—Cai You's 蔡攸 crime of leading the ruler into heterodoxy deserves execution. That the Mirror for Ministers…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
載此得非欲為臣者讀之毋渺毋林甫毋京毋
攸乎魏憲侯為相而四方灾變輒以上聞李文
靖為相而中外利害一切報罷似不同也然一
則恐人主逸欲而不知警懼一則恐少變舊制
而所傷實多事不同而忠同也秦檜力主和議
竟沮北伐之兵韓侂胄密議行兵欲為恢復之
計似有異也然一則當恢復之際而甘心事讎
一則當和議之後而邀功生事事雖異而惡不
異也竹頭木屑雖曰細事而陶侃綜理之周如
===
此可以親細務而少之乎柴塩利害雖曰盡言
而丁謂諂佞之罪如此可以能盡言而與之乎
嗟夫
聖人之制昭乎與日而並明蕩乎惟天之為大宜天
下之皆化矣而挾姦縱私傷仁敗德猶有厪執
事之憂得非以臣工徒能口
聖人之書而不能心其書乎愚願公卿之間不寶烏
號之弓而寶此書不藏曲阜之履而藏此帙申
明其制頒示中外使天下家讀其書人曉其義

而所傷實多其心則一而忠同也秦檜力主和議

而丁謂諂佞之罪如此可以䜟盡言而與之乎

號之弓而寶此書不藏曲阜之履而藏此帙申

punctuated: 載此，得非欲為臣者讀之，毋渺、毋林甫、毋京、毋攸乎？魏憲侯為相，而四方灾變輒以上聞；李文靖為相，而中外利害一切報罷，似不同也。然一則恐人主逸欲而不知警懼，一則恐少變舊制而所傷實多，事不同而忠同也。秦檜力主和議，竟沮北伐之兵；韓侂胄密議行兵，欲為恢復之計，似有異也。然一則當恢復之際而甘心事讎，一則當和議之後而邀功生事，事雖異而惡不異也。竹頭木屑，雖曰細事，而陶侃綜理之周如此，可以親細務而少之乎？柴塩利害，雖曰盡言，而丁謂諂佞之罪如此，可以能盡言而與之乎？嗟夫！聖人之制，昭乎與日而並明，蕩乎惟天之為大，宜天下之皆化矣，而挾姦縱私、傷仁敗德，猶有厪執事之憂，得非以臣工徒能口聖人之書，而不能心其書乎？愚願公卿之間，不寶烏號之弓而寶此書，不藏曲阜之履而藏此帙，申明其制，頒示中外，使天下家讀其書，人曉其義，
translation_en: … includes these accounts—could it not be because it desires those who serve as ministers to read them and not be like [Zhang]湯 [transcribed 渺, ?], [Li] Linfu, [Cai] Jing, or [Cai] You? When Marquis Xian of Wei [Bing Ji 丙吉? / Wei Xiang 魏相] served as Grand Councilor, he always reported natural disasters and anomalies from the four quarters to the throne; when Li Wenjing [Li Hang 李沆] served as Grand Councilor, wait—actually, Li Wenjing reported disasters whereas Wei Xiang reported everything, or vice versa: when Marquis Xian of Wei [Wei Xiang 魏相] served as Grand Councilor, he always reported disasters and anomalies from the four quarters to the throne, whereas when Li Wenjing [Li Hang 李沆] served as Grand Councilor, he rejected all proposals regarding advantages and disadvantages from inside and outside the court. They seem different. Yet the one feared that the ruler would indulge in ease and desires and fail to be vigilant and fearful, while the other feared that slightly altering old institutions would in fact cause great harm; their actions were different, but their loyalty was the same. Qin Gui vigorously advocated peace negotiations and ultimately blocked the northern expeditionary forces, whereas Han Tuozhou secretly deliberated on launching military campaigns in an attempt to plan for restoration. They seem distinct. Yet the one, at a moment suited for restoration, willingly served the enemy, while the other, after peace had been settled, sought merit and stirred up trouble; though their actions were distinct, their wickedness was no different. Bamboo ends and wood shavings may be called trivial matters, yet Tao Kan managed them with such thoroughness—can one belittle him for personally attending to petty affairs? The advantages and disadvantages of firewood and salt may be called speaking exhaustively, yet Ding Wei's crime of flattery and sycophancy was such as it was—can one approve of him for being able to speak exhaustively? Alas! The institutions of the Sage are as radiant as the sun and as vast as Heaven itself, so the whole world ought to have been transformed by them; yet harbouring deceit and indulging private interests, injuring benevolence and ruining virtue, still give cause for concern to Your Excellency. Could this not be because officials are merely able to recite the Sage's book with their mouths, without taking his book to heart? I wish that among the dukes and ministers, they would not treasure the Wuhao bow, but treasure this book; that they would not store away the shoes of Qufu, but store away this volume; and that its principles be reiterated and proclaimed inside and outside the court, causing every family in the empire to read this book and every person to understand its meaning, …

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
如聽
属車之音望
旄頭之塵自卓然興起其好善惡惡之心又何不
忠貞之懷循良之尚之足慮乎臣鑒所載善者
皆可法也乃所願學則范文正其人乎惟執事
進而教之幸甚
第二問
論天下之事無一定之勢處天下之事有一定
之理盖不同者勢也所同者理也君子持至一
===
之理御不一之勢此所以或寛或猛而同歸於
道也歟且讀捕蛇者說而知猛之不可觀蔓草
之戒又知寛之不可然則宜何如夫寛猛相濟
政是以和先儒許衡嘗有是言矣誠不易之論
也然其勢又有不同者明問謂周禮之用刑或
以輕或以重疑非相濟之道愚則曰政所以相
濟也彼因時而施者以教化有行否之異耳其
即吕刑世輕世重之典乎然孔明治蜀宜用輕
典也方承劉璋之暗威刑不肅蜀人自恣苟以

道也歟且讀捕蛇者說而知猛之不可觀萇草
之戒又知寬之不可然則宜何如夫寬猛相濟

即呂刑世輕世重之典乎然孔明治蜀宜用輕
典也方承劉璋之暗威刑不肅蜀人自恣苟以
punctuated:
如聽属車之音、望旄頭之塵，自卓然興起其好善惡惡之心，又何不忠貞之懷、循良之尚之足慮乎？《臣鑒》所載善者，皆可法也；乃所願學，則范文正其人乎！惟執事進而教之，幸甚。

第二問
論天下之事，無一定之勢；處天下之事，有一定之理。盖不同者，勢也；所同者，理也。君子持至一之理，御不一之勢，此所以或寛或猛，而同歸於道也歟！且讀《捕蛇者說》而知猛之不可，觀蔓草之戒又知寛之不可，然則宜何如？夫「寛猛相濟，政是以和」，先儒許衡嘗有是言矣，誠不易之論也。然其勢又有不同者。明問謂《周禮》之用刑，或以輕，或以重，疑非相濟之道。愚則曰：政所以相濟也。彼因時而施者，以教化有行否之異耳，其即《吕刑》「世輕世重」之典乎！然孔明治蜀，宜用輕典也。方承劉璋之暗，威刑不肅，蜀人自恣，苟以…
translation_en:
… as if listening to the sound of the imperial attendant carriages and gazing upon the dust of the Vanguard Banner, they will naturally and outstandingly rouse their hearts to love the good and hate the evil; what need would there be to worry that loyalty and rectitude would not be cherished, or that dutiful and良 benign governance would not be esteemed? The good men recorded in the Mirror for Ministers (Chenjian) are all worthy of emulation; yet as for the one I wish to take as my model, would it not be a man like Fan Wenzheng [Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹]! May Your Excellency bring me forward and instruct me—that would be my greatest fortune.

Question Two
In discussing the affairs of the world, there is no fixed circumstance; in managing the affairs of the world, there is a fixed principle. For what differs is circumstance, and what is the same is principle. The gentleman upholds the supremely unified principle to govern varying circumstances—is this not why, whether through leniency or through severity, both return alike to the Way? Moreover, when one reads the "Discourse on the Snake-Catcher" (Bushezhe shuo), one knows that severity is unacceptable; when one observes the warning about creeping weeds, one also knows that leniency is unacceptable. What, then, ought to be done? Now, "when leniency and severity complement each other, governance becomes harmonious"—the former Confucian scholar Xu Heng 許衡 once spoke these words [quoting the Zuo Tradition], and it is truly an immutable argument. Yet the circumstances may also differ. Your discerning question states that in the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) the application of punishments is sometimes light and sometimes heavy, and doubts whether this is the way of mutual complementation. I, however, say: this is precisely how governance achieves mutual complementation. That those punishments were applied according to the times was simply because of differences in whether moral transformation had taken effect or not—is this not the very statute of "lightening in some ages and weighting in others" in the "Punishments of Lü" (Lüxing)? Yet when Kongming [Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮] governed Shu, it ought to have been an occasion for applying the light statute. Having just succeeded the benighted rule of Liu Zhang 劉璋, when authority and punishments were not strict and the people of Shu were self-indulgent, if he had…

text:
寬濟之是以水濟水也故頗尚嚴峻而蜀中以
治裴度平蔡宜用重典也時當元濟之虐偶語
有禁過從者死苟以猛救之是以火加火也故
去其苛政而淮西以安是則輕重異施而皆治
者非相濟而然歟明問又謂或者之論治或以
寬或以嚴似非相濟之道愚亦曰政所以相濟
也彼因人而施者以其人有淑慝之别耳其它
虞書刑故宥小之義乎是以杭蜀之地號稱良
民急之則怨矣所謂保小民如保赤子故薛奎
===
蘇頌皆以寬稱開封京兆號為難治寬之則弛
矣所謂馭悍吏如馭悍馬故薛奎蘇頌皆以嚴
著是則前後異施而皆善者又非相濟而然歟
至若子產之告大叔以水狎則民玩火烈則民
畏故曰有德者能以寬服民其次莫如猛然時
乎嚴亦嚴豈可一於寬耶崔寔之論東漢謂四
牡橫奔皇路險傾故曰嚴之則治寬之則亂然
時乎寬亦寬豈可專於嚴耶使寬也有嚴以濟
之則大叔之悔可無也使嚴也有寬以濟之則

punctuated: 寬濟之，是以水濟水也，故頗尚嚴峻，而蜀中以治。裴度平蔡，宜用重典也，時當元濟之虐，偶語有禁，過從者死，苟以猛救之，是以火加火也，故去其苛政，而淮西以安。是則輕重異施而皆治者，非相濟而然歟？明問又謂或者之論治，或以寬，或以嚴，似非相濟之道。愚亦曰：政所以相濟也。彼因人而施者，以其人有淑慝之别耳，其它《虞書》刑故宥小之義乎？是以杭、蜀之地，號稱良民，急之則怨矣，所謂保小民如保赤子，故薛奎、蘇頌皆以寬稱；開封、京兆，號為難治，寬之則弛矣，所謂馭悍吏如馭悍馬，故薛奎、蘇頌皆以嚴著。是則前後異施而皆善者，又非相濟而然歟？至若子產之告大叔，以水狎則民玩，火烈則民畏，故曰：「有德者能以寬服民，其次莫如猛。」然時乎嚴亦嚴，豈可一於寬耶？崔寔之論東漢，謂「四牡橫奔，皇路險傾」，故曰：「嚴之則治，寬之則亂。」然時乎寬亦寬，豈可專於嚴耶？使寬也有嚴以濟之，則大叔之悔可無也；使嚴也有寬以濟之，則
translation_en:
… leniency, that would have been like adding water to water. Therefore, he placed considerable emphasis on strictness and severity, and through this the region of Shu was brought to order. When Pei Du 裴度 pacified Cai 蔡, one would expect heavy penalties to have been appropriate. Yet at that time the people had just suffered under the tyranny of [Wu] Yuanji 吳元濟, when whispering in pairs was forbidden and visiting one another was punishable by death. Had he sought to remedy the situation with severity, that would have been like adding fire to fire. Therefore, he abolished those harsh measures, and through this Huai-Xi 淮西 was brought to peace. Thus, when light and heavy measures were applied differently yet both resulted in good order, was this not because they complemented one another?

The enlightened question also notes that when certain commentators discuss governance, some advocate leniency while others advocate strictness, which would seem contrary to the principle of mutual complementation. To this I also reply: this is precisely how governance achieves mutual complementation. Those who tailor their measures to the people do so simply because people differ in being good or wicked. Is this not [?; 其它 for 其即] the meaning of punishing intentional offenses and pardoning minor ones in the Book of Yu (Yushu) [in the Book of Documents]? For this reason, the regions of Hangzhou 杭州 and Shu are renowned for having law-abiding people; if pressed too hard, they become resentful. As the saying goes, "Protect the common people as one protects an infant." Thus both Xue Kui 薛奎 and Su Song 蘇頌 were praised for their leniency there. Kaifeng 開封 and Jingzhao 京兆, by contrast, are notorious for being difficult to govern; if treated with leniency, they become lax. As the saying goes, "Control unruly subofficial functionaries as one controls an unruly horse." Thus both Xue Kui and Su Song became famous for their strictness there. When their earlier and later measures differed yet both proved admirable, was this not again because they complemented one another?

As for Zichan's 子產 advice to Taishu 大叔, he noted that because water is familiar, the people trifle with it, whereas because fire is fierce, the people fear it; hence he said, "Only the virtuous can subdue the people with leniency; for the next best, nothing surpasses severity." Yet when the occasion calls for strictness, even the virtuous will be strict—how could one rely exclusively on leniency? And when Cui Shi 崔寔 discussed the Eastern Han, he said that "the four-horse team bolts wildly, and the imperial road is perilous andtilting," and therefore concluded, "Treat it with strictness and there is order; treat it with leniency and there is chaos." Yet when the occasion calls for leniency, one should also be lenient—how could one rely solely on strictness? If leniency is complemented by strictness, then Taishu's regret can be avoided; if strictness is complemented by leniency, then …

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
郅都之譏何有哉此寬猛相濟所以為不易之
常道也洪惟我
朝紀綱法度井然而有條禮樂刑法四達而不悖
皆
祖宗之制垂憲萬世而無弊者也
列聖相承勵精圖治其大經大法一惟
成憲之是遵矣而小節細務施為緩急之間或因
其寬而濟之嚴以示戒懲或因其嚴而濟之寬
以廣矜恤固隨時制宜之道也然一法立則一
===
弊生不能無小過不及之可慮而弛張損益愚
何人斯而敢僭議乎雖然愚聞之書曰監于先
王成憲其永無愆詩曰不愆不忘率由舊章蓋
遵先王之法而過者未之有也政無小大亦惟
成憲之是法則寬猛自得其中而治化益臻於盛
又何過與不及之足患哉敢以是復明問惟執

punctuated:
郅都之譏何有哉？此寬猛相濟所以為不易之常道也。洪惟我朝，紀綱法度井然而有條，禮樂刑法四達而不悖，皆祖宗之制，垂憲萬世而無弊者也。列聖相承，勵精圖治，其大經大法一惟成憲之是遵矣。而小節細務，施為緩急之間，或因其寬而濟之嚴以示戒懲，或因其嚴而濟之寬以廣矜恤，固隨時制宜之道也。然一法立則一弊生，不能無小過、不及之可慮。而弛張損益，愚何人斯而敢僭議乎？雖然，愚聞之《書》曰：「監于先王成憲，其永無愆。」《詩》曰：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」蓋遵先王之法而過者，未之有也。政無小大，亦惟成憲之是法，則寬猛自得其中，而治化益臻於盛，又何過與不及之足患哉？敢以是復明問，惟執事進教之。

第三問
讀《洪範》「惟辟作福作威」之言，則知人君之大柄…
translation_en:
…what censure like that incurred by Zhi Du 郅都 could there ever have been? This is why tempering leniency and severity with each other is an immutable and constant principle.

Reflecting deeply upon our dynasty, its fundamental principles and legal institutions are well-ordered and systematic, and its rites, music, and penal laws reach in all four directions without contradiction. All of these are the institutions of our imperial ancestors, handed down as models for ten thousand generations without defect. The successive sage emperors have inherited them one after another, exerting themselves to achieve good governance; in great principles and fundamental laws, they have strictly abided by the established constitutions alone. Yet in minor details and routine affairs, in deciding whether to act with urgency or deliberation, sometimes in view of existing leniency they have tempered it with severity so as to display warning and chastisement, and sometimes in view of existing severity they have tempered it with leniency so as to broaden compassion and relief—this is indeed the way of adapting measures to the times. Nevertheless, whenever a law is established, an abuse arises, and one cannot be without concern over minor excesses or shortcomings. Yet as for relaxing or tightening, diminishing or augmenting, who am I, ignorant as I am, to dare presumptuously discuss such matters? Even so, I have heard that the Book of Documents (Shu 書) says: "Take as your mirror the established constitutions of the former kings, and you will forever be free from fault." And the Book of Odes (Shi 詩) says: "Neither erring nor forgetting, following the old statutes." Indeed, there has never been anyone who followed the laws of the former kings and yet fell into error. In governance, whether in matters great or small, if one takes only the established constitutions as the model, then leniency and severity will naturally attain their due mean, and transformative governance will increasingly reach perfection—what need will there be to worry about excess or deficiency? I venture to offer this in reply to your enlightened question, and pray that Your Excellency will grant me further instruction.

Third Question
When we read the words in the "Great Plan" (Hongfan 洪範), "It belongs to the sovereign alone to confer favors and to awe," we know that the great handle of authority of a ruler…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
固在於賞罰誦商頌賞不僭罰不濫之語又知
人君之賞罰尤在於至公甚矣賞罰者人主之
大柄也苟賞不當功罰不當罪則無以示勸懲
然則人君賞罰何可以不公哉思昔三代以上
之聖人何其刑賞之公如天地之無私覆也如
日月之無私照也此所以致治化之盛而非後
世所可及也三代以下君學不傳倏而公倏而
私而公私之相勝暫而明暫而晦而明晦之相
剥於是刑賞之得失相半矣漢之高帝宣帝七
===
===
制之優也怨雍齒而什方以侯戮丁公而人臣
無效黃霸以寛和而拜相嚴延年以殘酷而棄
市此亦一時之天理也然審食其以嬖倖而封
韓彭以元功而戮王成偽增戶口而侯以關內
蓋寛饒數犯上意而剄於闕下其心又蔽矣唐
之太宗憲宗三宗之主也知魏徵之賢不以仇
讐而不用知裴寂之貪不以故舊而不斥討李
錡積年之叛相李絳鯁直之臣此亦一時之天
理也然宇文士及以諛佞而見擢李君羨以讖

===

無效黄霸以寬和而拜相嚴延年以殘酷而棄
市此亦一時之天理也然審食其以嬖倖而封
韓彭以元功而戮王成僞增户口而侯以關内
蓋寬饒數犯上意而刭於闕下其心又蔽矣唐

理也然宇文士及以諛佞而見擢李君羨以讖
punctuated: 固在於賞罰；誦《商頌》「賞不僭，罰不濫」之語，又知人君之賞罰尤在於至公。甚矣，賞罰者，人主之大柄也！苟賞不當功，罰不當罪，則無以示勸懲。然則人君賞罰，何可以不公哉！思昔三代以上之聖人，何其刑賞之公？如天地之無私覆也，如日月之無私照也。此所以致治化之盛，而非後世所可及也。三代以下，君學不傳，倏而公，倏而私，而公私之相勝；暫而明，暫而晦，而明晦之相剥。於是刑賞之得失相半矣。漢之高帝、宣帝，七制之優也。怨雍齒而什方以侯，戮丁公而人臣無效；黃霸以寛和而拜相，嚴延年以殘酷而棄市，此亦一時之天理也。然審食其以嬖倖而封，韓、彭以元功而戮；王成偽增戶口而侯以關內，蓋寛饒數犯上意而剄於闕下，其心又蔽矣。唐之太宗、憲宗，三宗之主也。知魏徵之賢，不以仇讐而不用；知裴寂之貪，不以故舊而不斥；討李錡積年之叛，相李絳鯁直之臣，此亦一時之天理也。然宇文士及以諛佞而見擢，李君羨以讖
translation_en: …indeed lies in rewards and punishments; and when one recites the words of the Sacrificial Odes of Shang (Shang song), "Rewards were not excessive, punishments were not abusive," one further understands that a ruler's rewards and punishments depend above all on the utmost impartiality. Great indeed are rewards and punishments as the supreme authority of the sovereign! If rewards do not match merits and punishments do not match crimes, there is no way to demonstrate encouragement and warning. How then could a ruler's rewards and punishments be anything less than impartial? When we reflect upon the sages of the Three Dynasties and earlier, how impartial were their punishments and rewards! They were like Heaven and Earth covering all without partiality, and like the sun and moon shining on all without partiality. This is how they achieved the flourishing of good governance and transformation, which later ages have been unable to reach. After the Three Dynasties, the learning of the ruler was no longer transmitted. Suddenly impartial, suddenly selfish, impartiality and selfishness contended for dominance; briefly clear, briefly obscured, clarity and obscurity eroded one another. Consequently, the successes and failures of punishments and rewards were equal in measure. In the Han dynasty, Emperor Gao (Gaodi) and Emperor Xuan (Xuandi) were the finest of the seven rulers who established enduring institutions. Though Emperor Gao resented Yong Chi 雍齒, he enfeoffed him as Marquis of Shifang; by executing Lord Ding (Ding Gong 丁公), he ensured that no subject would imitate his disloyalty. Under Emperor Xuan, Huang Ba 黃霸 was appointed Grand Councilor for his leniency and harmony, while Yan Yannian 嚴延年 was executed in the marketplace for his cruelty and harshness. This too was the Principle of Heaven manifesting for a time. Yet Shen Yiji 審食其 was enfeoffed as a favored minion, while Han Xin 韓信 and Peng Yue 彭越 were executed despite their supreme merits; Wang Cheng 王成 falsified population increases and was made a Marquis Within the Passes, while Gai Kuanrao 蓋寬饒 repeatedly offended the emperor's wishes and cut his own throat beneath the palace gates—here their minds were once again obscured. In the Tang dynasty, Emperor Taizong and Emperor Xianzong were two of the "Three Ancestors" (sanzong). Taizong recognized the worthiness of Wei Zheng 魏徵 and did not refuse to employ him on account of old enmity; he knew the greed of Pei Ji 裴寂 and did not fail to dismiss him on account of old friendship. Xianzong suppressed the long-standing rebellion of Li Qi 李錡 and appointed the outspoken and upright minister Li Jiang 李絳 as Grand Councilor. This too was the Principle of Heaven manifesting for a time. Yet Yuwen Shiji 宇文士及 was promoted for his flattery and sycophancy, and Li Junxian 李君羨 was on account of prognostic…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
語而見誅皇甫鎛事聚斂而至相位韓文公諫
佛骨而貶潮陽其心則又蔽矣故先儒論漢唐
之君以為有一分之天理固足以立一分之事
功有一分之私欲亦足以召一分之事變殆謂
此也洪惟
聖天子即位以来奉三無私以壹有衆未明求衣惟
刑賞是公丙枕不寐惟刑賞是明是心也非即
大舜功疑惟重之心乎非即文王勿誤庶獄之
心乎然日月之明也照有不及天地之大也人
===
猶有憾故濫殺無辜以要功冒作功次以申請
而賞或不能無失矣愚以為若此者不與之固
不可遂與之尤不可惟當申重總督之任嚴
勅紀功之官考其某處也有某功某功也有某驗
必驗功得實而後賞加焉其不然者則有殺降
之罪有面欺之誅人其敢乎羅織成罪上下其
手而刑或不能無失矣愚以為若此者遂宥之
固不可遂殺之尤不可惟當申命典獄之官戒
飭廷評之職使推鞫窮詰以原其情詳明法意

punctuated: 語而見誅，皇甫鎛事聚斂而至相位，韓文公諫佛骨而貶潮陽，其心則又蔽矣。故先儒論漢、唐之君，以為有一分之天理，固足以立一分之事功；有一分之私欲，亦足以召一分之事變，殆謂此也。洪惟聖天子即位以来，奉三無私以壹有衆；未明求衣，惟刑賞是公；丙枕不寐，惟刑賞是明。是心也，非即大舜功疑惟重之心乎？非即文王勿誤庶獄之心乎？然日月之明也，照有不及；天地之大也，人猶有憾。故濫殺無辜以要功，冒作功次以申請，而賞或不能無失矣。愚以為若此者，不與之固不可，遂與之尤不可；惟當申重總督之任，嚴勅紀功之官，考其某處也有某功，某功也有某驗，必驗功得實而後賞加焉。其不然者，則有殺降之罪，有面欺之誅，人其敢乎？羅織成罪，上下其手，而刑或不能無失矣。愚以為若此者，遂宥之固不可，遂殺之尤不可；惟當申命典獄之官，戒飭廷評之職，使推鞫窮詰以原其情，詳明法意…
translation_en:
…prophetic sayings and was executed; Huangfu Bo 皇甫鎛 engaged in predatory exactions and yet rose to the position of Grand Councilor; Han Yu (Han Wengong 韓文公) remonstrated against the Buddha's bone relic and was banished to Chaoyang 潮陽—their minds were once again obscured. Therefore, when former Confucian scholars discussed the rulers of the Han and Tang dynasties, they held that having one measure of Heavenly Principle is indeed sufficient to establish one measure of practical achievement, while having one measure of selfish desire is likewise sufficient to invite one measure of political disorder; they were surely referring to this.

Reflecting with awe upon our Sacred Son of Heaven, since ascending the throne he has upheld the "threefold impartiality" (san wusi 三無私) to unify the multitude. Calling for his robes before dawn, he seeks only impartiality in punishments and rewards; sleepless on his pillow in the third watch of the night, he seeks only clarity in punishments and rewards. This mind—is it not the very mind of Great Shun 大舜, who rewarded generously even when merit was in doubt? Is it not the very mind of King Wen 文王, who sought never to err in the multitude of judicial cases? Yet as bright as the sun and moon are, there are places their light does not reach; as vast as heaven and earth are, people still find things to regret in them. Thus, when some indiscriminately slaughter the innocent to claim credit, or fraudulently fabricate grades of merit to petition for advancement, rewards perhaps cannot be entirely free from error. In my humble opinion, in cases such as these, simply withholding the reward is certainly unacceptable, yet immediately granting it is even more unacceptable. Rather, one ought to reaffirm the heavy responsibilities of the Supreme Commanders (zongdu 總督) and strictly charge the Merit-Recording Officials (jigong zhi guan 紀功之官) to investigate what specific merit was achieved at what specific place, and what specific verification exists for each merit; only after the merit is verified and the facts established should rewards be conferred. As for those who act otherwise, there is the crime of slaughtering those who have surrendered, and the punishment for deceiving the sovereign to his face—would anyone then dare to do so?

When others fabricate charges to frame the innocent and manipulate the law at will, punishments perhaps cannot be entirely free from error. In my humble opinion, in cases such as these, immediately pardoning the accused is certainly unacceptable, yet immediately executing them is even more unacceptable. Rather, one ought to reiterate orders to the officials in charge of prisons and admonish those holding the office of Judicial Investigator of the Court of Judicial Review (tingping 廷評), causing them to interrogate thoroughly to ascertain the true circumstances, and to carefully clarify the intent of the law…

title: 成化十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以定其罪必情罪相應而後罰加焉其不然者
正以故出故入之條律以受囑枉法之罪刑其
濫乎草茅有懷思欲獻之吾
君吾相而無由執事先生倘有取於負暄之愚上裨
廟謨之萬一亦豈非仁人君子之心哉
第四問
有儒者之學術必有儒者之事功儒者之道其
大矣哉詩書禮樂其業也仁義禮智其蘊也齊
家治國平天下其用也以之為上則為德以之
===
為下則為民以之為天下則無所不宜而況於
為吏乎況於為將乎自儒學不明俎豆軍旅分
為二途俗吏迂儒互相攻呵將之鄙儒則曰措
大吏之鄙儒則曰迂腐噫儒道果若是小耶儒
道與天地竝而不行則非一日矣彼子游學道
愛人而絃歌以化武城子賤尊賢取友而彈琴
以治單父儒者之效亦畧見於吏已若文翁治
蜀郡而首興學校兒寬以經術而潤飾吏事劉
昆之仁及猛虎韓愈之信孚鱷魚則儒者之粗
